title: Track 7, Lesson 6: Rebalancing - holding the risk level you actually chose
subtitle: Without rebalancing, your portfolio drifts away from the risk level you originally picked.
whyItMatters: After a few years without rebalancing, the "70% shares - 30% bonds" portfolio you started with may have become 85%-15%, purely because shares rose faster - leaving you carrying more risk than you ever chose, without noticing.
openingQuestion: You start with a portfolio of 60% shares / 40% bonds. After 3 years, shares have risen so far that the split is now 75%/25%. What should you do?
openingOptions: Sell some shares, buy bonds, and return to about 60/40
Borrow money from the bank to buy even more shares while the market is rising well
Do nothing at all and leave the current split, since shares are on a good upward trend
Sell every bond and move entirely into shares, because they are rising strongly
explanation: Rebalancing means periodically adjusting the portfolio back to its target weights. When shares rise faster than bonds, the share weight climbs by itself - and if you never correct it, you are carrying more risk than the level you once judged appropriate for your own risk tolerance.

diagram.label: The weights drift from the original target
Sell some of what rose, buy more of what lagged

realWorldExample.description: Professional funds typically rebalance on a schedule (quarterly or annually) or whenever the weights drift past a set threshold (5 percentage points, say) - a required discipline in professional portfolio management rather than something done on a whim.

quiz.question: What does rebalancing force an investor to do, with discipline?
options: Leave everything alone and simply record the new weights
Sell the weak assets and buy more of the rising ones
Sell some of what has risen, and buy more of what lagged
Add new money into whichever asset class is rising
quiz.explanation: Rebalancing has a useful side effect: it forces you to sell some of what has risen a long way (usually when the price is high) and buy more of what is relatively weak (usually when the price is lower) - the opposite of the natural instinct to buy more of whatever is going up.

quiz.question: Your target is 50% Vietnamese shares, 30% international shares, 20% bonds. After 2 years the actual split is 60%/25%/15%. What is the correct rebalancing action?
options: Leave it, since a 10% drift is not significant
Sell bonds and buy more Vietnamese shares, which are performing well
Sell all three holdings and buy back from scratch at the target weights
Sell some Vietnamese shares, buy more international shares and bonds
quiz.explanation: Correct rebalancing adjusts EVERY part that has drifted: cutting what has overshot (Vietnamese shares 60%→50%) and topping up what has fallen short (international 25%→30%, bonds 15%→20%) - returning the whole portfolio to the split originally chosen for your risk tolerance.

quiz.question: Why does a portfolio drift from its target weights over time?
options: Because different asset classes rise and fall at different rates over each period
Because brokerages automatically adjust portfolio weights every quarter
Because management fees are deducted unevenly across the different asset classes held
Because investors are required to add money to whichever asset is falling
quiz.explanation: The weights change while nobody does anything: shares rising 30% while bonds stand still turns a 70/30 portfolio into 76/24 on its own. Your risk has gone up without you ever deciding it should.

quiz.question: What is the cheapest way to rebalance for someone still accumulating?
options: Sell the entire portfolio and buy it back at the original target weights
Use new contributions to top up what is short, rather than selling what is over
Only rebalance once the weights have drifted more than fifty percent from target
Move everything to cash at year end and reallocate at the start of the next year
quiz.explanation: Topping up what is short triggers no transfer tax and does not touch the positions currently in profit. For anyone still contributing monthly, this is usually enough to keep the portfolio on track.

quiz.question: How far should the weights drift before you rebalance?
options: Only a drift of more than thirty percentage points calls for any adjustment
Any drift at all, however small, should be corrected back immediately
About five percentage points from target is the level commonly used
There is no threshold - rebalance only on the last day of each year
quiz.explanation: Too sensitive and you pay fees and tax on adjustments that were never needed; too infrequent and the portfolio drifts far from the risk level you chose. Around five percentage points is the level much of the literature recommends.

quiz.question: Does rebalancing increase long-run returns?
options: No, rebalancing always reduces returns because of the trading fees involved
Yes, rebalancing always raises returns because it forces you to buy in cheaply
Yes, because it keeps the portfolio holding whichever asset is rising fastest
Not necessarily - the point is controlling risk, not returns
quiz.explanation: Through a long bull market in shares, rebalancing can even lower returns, because you keep trimming the winner. What it guarantees is that the portfolio does not quietly become riskier than you can accept.

keyTakeaways: Not rebalancing lets a portfolio drift from the risk level you chose - usually towards more risk while markets rise
Rebalancing is disciplined 'sell high, buy low', running against the natural instinct
Set a rebalancing schedule (annually) or a drift threshold (5 percentage points, say) rather than acting on a whim

practicePrompt.question: Your target is 70% shares, 30% bonds. After 4 years of strong markets the actual split has become 88% shares, 12% bonds without your knowing, because you never checked. What does that mean?
options: The portfolio has drifted from the risk level you originally chose, and drifted towards distinctly more risk (88% shares now)
There is nothing wrong at all, because a higher share weighting always means your portfolio is performing better than you expected
You should keep the 88/12 split as it is, because this proves that the original investment strategy was entirely correct
You need to sell all your shares immediately and move everything into bonds in order to correct this drift in the weights
practicePrompt.explanation: Not rebalancing lets a portfolio drift from the risk level originally chosen, usually towards more risk while markets rise - the fix is rebalancing back to 70/30, not selling all the shares.

summary.keyIdea: Not rebalancing lets a portfolio drift from the risk level you chose - usually towards more risk while markets rise
summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Rebalancing is disciplined 'sell high, buy low', running against the natural instinct

application.title: Check it now
application.message: Compare the current share/bond weights in your portfolio with the target you originally set - if the drift is more than 5 percentage points, it is time to rebalance.
application.secondary: Rebalancing is disciplined selling high and buying low, even though it feels backwards.

sections.text: You once chose an asset allocation that suited your risk tolerance - 70% shares, 30% bonds, say. But without deliberate correction, that split drifts over time, and you may be carrying far more risk than you ever agreed to.
Why a portfolio drifts from its target

When shares rise faster than bonds through a favourable stretch, the share weight swells on its own without you doing anything. A target of 50% Vietnamese shares / 30% international shares / 20% bonds can become 60%/25%/15% after two strong years in the domestic market - and your real risk is now above the level you chose from your own risk tolerance.
Rebalancing is disciplined 'sell high, buy low'

To bring that portfolio back to 50%/30%/20%, the correct action is: sell some Vietnamese shares (60% → 50%, the part that rose most), and use the proceeds to buy more international shares (25% → 30%) and bonds (15% → 20%) - the parts that are relatively weaker. In substance you are selling some of what is expensive and buying more of what is relatively cheap - the exact opposite of the natural instinct to buy more of whatever is surging.

Professional funds and pension funds typically rebalance on a fixed schedule (quarterly or annually) or whenever the weights drift past a set threshold, such as 5 percentage points. It is a required discipline rather than a matter of mood - and retail investors should apply the same principle instead of letting emotion decide when to adjust.

items: Set a fixed rebalancing date, for instance once a year on the same day
Or use a drift threshold (5 percentage points from target, say) to trigger it whenever it happens
Adjust EVERY part that has drifted, not only the one that drifted most
Weigh trading costs and tax when rebalancing - there is no need to hit every percentage point exactly
Don't let emotion (regret at selling a rising holding) interfere with the decision
